summary: Explains why the IAB believes that, when the interests of end users conflict with those of other parties, IETF decisions should favor end users. It also explores how the IETF can more effectively achieve this. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8890 asks a simple question about standards work: when the interests of ordinary Internet users clash with those of other groups, whose side should the standards body take? The IAB answers that it should be the users' side, and the RFC explains what it means to be an end user, why this matters, and five practical ways to put the answer into practice.

questions: why is the internet for end users
what does the iab say about end users
how should the ietf make decisions about standards
subtitle: Why the IAB says standards work should favour the people who use the Internet, and how it thinks that can be done.

tldr.problem: Standards bodies make decisions that look purely technical, but the choices they make decide what is possible on the Internet, and those choices can serve one group at the expense of another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines what it means by an end user, sets out why the IETF should favour them when interests conflict, and then gives five concrete ways to do that, from consulting affected communities to designing systems that keep power away from the network operator.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a statement of position from the Internet Architecture Board rather than a specification, and it asks for negative effects on end users to be identified and mitigated rather than left unexamined.

today: RFC 8890 is an Informational document from August 2020, a statement of position by the Internet Architecture Board rather than a specification. No RFC obsoletes or updates it, so it stands as the IAB's published answer to the question of whom standards work is for.

sections.title: The Question the IAB Is Asking
sections.content:
Many who participate in the IETF are most comfortable making what are believed to be purely technical decisions; the process favours technical merit through the well-known mantra of rough consensus and running code.

Nevertheless, the running code that results from the process, when things work well, inevitably has an impact beyond technical considerations, because the underlying decisions afford some uses while discouraging others. While the participants believe they are making only technical decisions, in reality they are defining, in some degree, what is possible on the Internet itself.

This impact has become significant. As the Internet increasingly mediates essential functions in societies, it has unavoidably become profoundly political: it has helped people overthrow governments, revolutionize social orders, swing elections, control populations, collect data about individuals and reveal secrets. It has created wealth for some individuals and companies while destroying that of others.

All of this raises the question of for whom the community goes through the pain of gathering rough consensus and writing running code. There are a variety of parties that standards can benefit, such as end users, network operators, schools, equipment vendors, specification authors, specification implementers, content owners, governments, nongovernmental organizations, social movements, employers and parents. Successful specifications will provide some benefit to all the relevant parties, because standards do not represent a zero-sum game. However, there are sometimes situations where there is a conflict between the needs of two or more parties.

In those situations, when one of the parties is an end user of the Internet, for example a person using a web browser, a mail client or another agent that connects to the Internet, the IAB argues that the IETF should favour their interests over those of other parties.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol decision is never only about the protocol. Deciding how a header is laid out also decides which uses of the network are easy and which are hard, and that shapes who benefits. The IAB says the group that should benefit is the people who use the Internet, and this RFC explains why and what follows from that.

sections.title: Who Counts as an End User
sections.content:
In this document, end users means human users whose activities IETF standards support, sometimes indirectly. The end user of a protocol to manage routers is therefore not a router administrator; it is the people using the network that the router operates within.

End users are not necessarily a homogeneous group. They might have different views of how the Internet should work, and they might occupy several roles, such as a seller, buyer, publisher, reader, service provider and consumer. An end user might browse the Web, monitor remote equipment, play a game, videoconference with colleagues, send messages to friends, or perform an operation in a remote surgery theater. They might be at the keyboard, or represented by software indirectly, for example as a daemon.

An individual end user might have many interests, such as privacy, security, flexibility and reachability, that are sometimes in tension. A person whose interests need to be considered might not be directly using a specific system connected to the Internet. A child using a browser has parents or guardians whose interests may be relevant. A person pictured in a photograph may have an interest in the systems that process that photograph, and a person entering a room with sensors that send data to the Internet may have interests involved in deliberations about how those sensor readings are handled. While such less direct interactions are harder to evaluate, the concept of an end user in this document includes such people.
sections.plainLanguage: An end user is a person whose activities the standards support, directly or not. That is not the network engineer running the router, it is everyone who depends on it. A person may be several end users at once, playing the part of buyer, publisher and consumer, and their own interests, privacy on one side and reachability on the other, can pull in different directions.

sections.title: Why the IETF Should Prioritize End Users
sections.content:
Even before the IETF was established, the Internet technical community focused on user needs, at least since RFC 1, which stated that one of the goals must be to stimulate the immediate and easy use by a wide class of users.

While the community specializes in technical matters, the IETF is not neutral about the purpose of its work. In the mission statement of RFC 3935, the definitions include the statement that the IETF community wants the Internet to succeed because its existence and influence on economics, communication and education will help build a better human society. Later, in the same document, under the scope of the Internet, it says that the Internet is not value-neutral and neither is the IETF, and that the IETF wants the Internet to be useful for communities that share its commitment to openness and fairness, embracing technical concepts such as decentralized control, edge-user empowerment and sharing of resources, because those concepts resonate with the core values of the community and have little to do with the technology that is possible and much to do with the technology that is chosen to be created.

In other words, the IETF develops and maintains the Internet to promote the social good, and the society it is trying to enhance is composed of end users, along with groups of them forming businesses, governments, clubs, civil society organizations and other institutions. Merely advancing the measurable success of the Internet, in terms of deployment size, bandwidth, latency or number of users, is not an adequate goal, because that ignores how technology is so often used as a lever to assert power over users rather than to empower them.

Beyond fulfilling the mission, prioritizing end users helps ensure the long-term health of the Internet and the relevance of the IETF to it. Perceptions of capture by vendors or other providers harm both, and the IETF's work will, deservedly, lose end users' trust if it prioritizes, or is perceived to prioritize, others' interests over them. Ultimately the Internet will succeed or fail based on the actions of its end users, because they are the driving force behind its growth to date, and not prioritizing them jeopardizes the network effect that the Internet relies upon to provide so much value.
sections.plainLanguage: The reason to favour end users is not sentiment. The mission statement of the IETF already commits it to building the Internet for the good of society, and the people who make up society are the users. A network that is technically successful but that hands power to whoever operates it does not keep the trust of the people who depend on it, and that trust is what the Internet's value rests on.

sections.title: Engaging the Internet Community
sections.content:
The IETF community has no unique insight into what is good for end users, and it is often at a disadvantage because of its close understanding of some, but not all, aspects of the Internet. At the same time, it has a culture of considerable deference to a broader Internet community, roughly what the document calls end users, in its decision-making processes. Mere deference, however, is not adequate: even with the best intentions, the community cannot assume that its experiences of the Internet are those of all its end users, or that its decisions have a positive impact on them.

So there is a responsibility both to analyze the impacts of the work and to consult with the wider Internet community, in particular when a decision has a potential impact on end users. There are significant hurdles to doing so: the work is specialized and often esoteric, the processes for developing standards involve very long timescales, affected parties are rarely technical experts, and they often base their understanding of the Internet on incomplete, and sometimes inaccurate, models. Often, even when the community tries to engage a broader audience, their participation is minimal, until a change affects someone in a way they do not like. Surprising the Internet community is rarely a good outcome.

Government-sponsored individuals sometimes participate, which is welcome, but should not be taken as automatically representative of end users elsewhere, or even of all end users in the relevant jurisdiction. Civil society organizations that specialize in technology and Internet policy rarely participate broadly and are not necessarily representative of the larger community, but their understanding of end-user needs is often profound and they are in many ways the best-informed advocates for end-user concerns, so they should be considered a primary channel for engaging the broader community. A promising approach is to identify and engage specifically affected communities when making decisions that might affect them, for example industry associations, user groups or a set of individuals, and not to require them to come to the IETF: unless a stakeholder community is already engaged effectively, the community should explore meeting with them on their terms, taking the initiative to contact them, explain the work and solicit feedback.

Workshops, BOFs and Bar BOFs can gather input within the community, but rarely have the visibility into other communities required to solicit input. An event may be more effective if co-located with, or ideally hosted or co-hosted by, a forum familiar to that stakeholder community, and the IETF should raise the visibility of its work in such fora through conference talks, panels and newsletter articles. The IAB ESCAPE workshop is given as an example: it solicited input from Internet publishers and advertisers about a proposal that might affect them, and while the workshop was considered successful, participation might have been improved by identifying an appropriate industry forum and working with them to host the event. The community should also identify tailored feedback mechanisms, since subscribing to a mailing list may not be appropriate, and assure that they are well known in those communities. The Internet Society can be an invaluable partner here. Finally, the RFC Series contains Requests For Comments, so if there are serious implications of the work, the implications should be documented and feedback requested from the Internet community.
sections.plainLanguage: Consulting users is harder than it sounds, because the people affected are rarely protocol experts and rarely notice a proposal until it bites them. The RFC says the standards community should go to them rather than waiting, and hold events where the affected community already gathers.

sections.title: Creating User-Focused Systems
sections.content:
The community should pay particular attention to the kinds of architectures it creates, and to whether they encourage or discourage an Internet that works for end users.

One of the most successful Internet applications is the Web, which uses the HTTP application protocol. One of the key implementation roles in HTTP is that of the web browser, called the user agent in RFC 7230 and other specifications. User agents act as intermediaries between a service and the end user: rather than downloading an executable program from a service that has arbitrary access into the user's system, the user agent allows only limited access to display content and run code in a sandboxed environment. End users are diverse, and the ability of a few user agents to represent individual interests properly is imperfect, but this arrangement is an improvement over the alternative, which is the need to trust a website completely with all information on the system in order to browse it.

Defining the user agent role in standards also creates a virtuous cycle. It allows multiple implementations, allowing end users to switch between them at relatively low cost, although there are concerns about the complexity of the Web creating barriers to entry for new implementations. This creates an incentive for implementers to consider users' needs carefully, and those needs are often reflected in the defining standards. The resulting ecosystem still has many problems, but a distinguished user agent role provides an opportunity to improve it.

In contrast, the Internet of Things has not yet seen the broad adoption of a similar role. Many current systems require opaque, vendor-specific software or hardware for the user-facing component, and perhaps as a result that ecosystem and its end users face serious challenges.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser is the counter-example that works. It stands between the user and the site, runs the site's code in a sandbox and gives it only limited access, and because the role is written into the standard, anyone can build one. A device that instead needs the manufacturer's own software to be used has not gained that protection, and the RFC suggests that is where the trouble starts.

sections.title: Negative Impact, Conflicting Needs and Internal Wants
sections.content:
At its best, the work will unambiguously build a better human society. Sometimes it will be consciously neutral and open-ended, allowing the tussle among stakeholders to produce a range of results. At the very least, however, the community must examine its work for negative impact on end users and take steps to mitigate it. In particular, when a conflict between the interests of end users and other stakeholders has been identified, the community should err on the side of protecting end users.

Negative impact on end users is not defined in the document; that is something the relevant body, such as a working group, needs to discuss and reach consensus on. Merely asserting that something is harmful is not adequate. The converse is also true: it is not good practice to avoid identifying harms, nor is it acceptable to ignore them when brought to the IAB's attention. The IAB and IETF have already established a body of guidance for situations where this conflict is common, including RFC 7754 on filtering, RFC 7258 and RFC 7624 on pervasive surveillance, RFC 7288 on host firewalls and RFC 6973 on privacy considerations. Much of that advice has focused on maintaining the end-to-end properties of a connection, but that does not mean the responsibility to end users stops there: data collection by various applications even inside otherwise secure connections is a major problem on the Internet today, and inappropriate concentration of power on the Internet has become a concerning phenomenon on which protocol design might have some influence.

When the needs of different end users conflict, and both sets of end users have reasonable desires, the aim is again to minimize negative impact. When a decision improves the Internet for end users in one jurisdiction but at the cost of potential harm to others elsewhere, that is not a good trade-off; the Internet is designed for the pessimal environment, because if a user can be harmed, they probably will be, somewhere. There may be cases where genuine technical need requires compromise, but such trade-offs are carefully examined and avoided when there are alternate means of achieving the desired goals, and if they cannot be avoided, the choices and the reasoning ought to be thoroughly documented.

Finally, there are needs that are very visible to specification authors but that should explicitly not be prioritized over the needs of end users. These include convenience for document editors, IETF process matters, and architectural purity for its own sake.
sections.plainLanguage: Even when the intent is neutral, some decisions will end up helping one group and hurting another, and the community is expected to look for that and correct it. When two users' legitimate needs clash, the design should assume the worse case rather than the best, and any compromise forced by a genuine technical need should be written down with its reasoning.

viz.caption: WHAT AN END USER MIGHT BE DOING

items.title: Browse the Web
items.text: The classic case, with a browser acting between the user and the site.

items.title: Monitor remote equipment
items.text: Sensors and equipment that send data to the Internet on the user's behalf.

items.title: Play a game or videoconference
items.text: Interactive uses where delay and fairness between users matter.

items.title: Send messages
items.text: A person writing to friends, with interests in privacy and in reachability that may pull against each other.

items.title: Act through software
items.text: A daemon acting for a person, or a child browsing with parents whose interests also count.

items.title: Be represented in a system
items.text: A person in a photograph, or in a room with sensors, has interests in how that data is handled.

viz.caption: FIVE WAYS TO PUT END USERS FIRST

items.title: Engage the community
items.text: Go to the affected people rather than waiting for them, and hold events where they already gather.

items.title: Create user-focused systems
items.text: Favour architectures that keep control with the user, as the browser role does.

items.title: Identify negative impact
items.text: Look for harm to end users, discuss it, and err on the side of protecting them.

items.title: Handle conflicting needs
items.text: Design for the worst case, not the best one, and document any compromise that is forced.

items.title: Deprioritize internal needs
items.text: Do not put editor convenience, process matters or architectural purity above the user's interests.

viz.caption: THE USER AGENT ROLE AND ITS ABSENCE

left.title: The user agent
left.desc: A browser stands between the site and the person: limited access, code in a sandbox, and an open role that anyone can implement.
